title: Why some salts dissolve in acid

stimulus.title: Two salts and some acid
stimulus.text:
A student places excess solid calcium carbonate, CaCO₃, in one beaker of water and excess solid silver bromide, AgBr, in another, and stirs until each solution is saturated. The student then adds 1.0 M HNO₃ dropwise to each beaker.

CaCO₃(s) ⇌ Ca²⁺(aq) + CO₃²⁻(aq)    AgBr(s) ⇌ Ag⁺(aq) + Br⁻(aq)

The Ka of HCO₃⁻ is 4.7 × 10⁻¹¹. HBr is a strong acid.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: More CaCO₃ dissolves as the acid is added. Explain why, referring to Q and Ksp.

rubric.point: H₃O⁺ reacts with CO₃²⁻ (the conjugate base of the weak acid HCO₃⁻) to form HCO₃⁻, lowering [CO₃²⁻]
Q = [Ca²⁺][CO₃²⁻] falls below Ksp, so more solid dissolves until Q = Ksp

parts.sample: Carbonate is the conjugate base of the very weak acid HCO₃⁻, so it reacts with the added acid: CO₃²⁻ + H₃O⁺ → HCO₃⁻ + H₂O. This lowers [CO₃²⁻], so Q = [Ca²⁺][CO₃²⁻] becomes less than Ksp, and more CaCO₃ dissolves until Q equals Ksp again.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: The amount of AgBr that dissolves does not change noticeably. Explain why.

rubric.point: Br⁻ is the conjugate base of a strong acid and does not react with H₃O⁺, so [Br⁻] and Q are unchanged

parts.sample: Br⁻ is the conjugate base of the strong acid HBr, so it does not react with H₃O⁺. [Br⁻] stays the same, Q is unchanged, and no extra AgBr dissolves.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: A student claims the acid dissolves CaCO₃ because it increases the value of Ksp. Is the claim correct? Justify your answer.

rubric.point: No: Ksp depends only on temperature; the acid lowers Q by removing CO₃²⁻
accept: Ksp is constant at constant temperature

parts.sample: No. Ksp is an equilibrium constant and changes only with temperature. The acid changes Q, by removing carbonate, not Ksp.
